name: Proportionality bias
statement: Proportionality bias is the tendency to infer that an event with large consequences must have had a large cause, offered as one reason conspiracy explanations appeal.
meaning: The claim is about a single inference, not about conspiracy theories as a class. A person learns how big an outcome was and reads the size of the cause off it, in cases where the outcome carries no information about the cause. Whether a computer crash cost a student his job, or whether a president survived the shot, is settled by things that happened after the event and cannot bear on what started it. Two literatures test this. One studies causal judgement directly and calls it consequence-cause matching or cause-effect magnitude correspondence, using diseases, plane faults, negotiations and tornadoes. The other studies conspiracy belief and calls it the major event, major cause heuristic. The reasoning step is the same in both, and the results are not. Illusory pattern perception, treated under apophenia, is a different claim: it is about seeing structure in noise rather than about matching a cause to an outcome already known.

origin.who: Patrick J. Leman and Marco Cinnirella
origin.note: The paper that gave the idea its slogan. Its abstract reports 64 participants reading one of four variations on a vignette about the assassination or attempted assassination of a hypothetical president, then rating how likely each of eight statements was. Endorsement of a conspiracy account was higher when the president died than when he survived, and levels of belief in real-world conspiracy theories did not relate to that inference. The earlier antecedent is McCauley and Jacques, in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology in 1979. Neither paper's full text was obtained for this entry.

evidence: The largest reported effects are in the causal-judgement literature rather than the conspiracy one. Spina's 2009 Queen's University dissertation, published the following year with Ji, Guo, Zhang, Li and Fabrigar, gave 59 European-Canadian and 60 Chinese students a disease outbreak that either killed people or hospitalised them, followed by a highly infectious or a standard strain of bacteria. Participants tied the high-magnitude effect to the high-magnitude cause, 7.73 against 4.05 on a nine-point scale, and the low-magnitude effect to the low-magnitude cause, 6.82 against 3.72, an interaction of F(1, 115) = 160.18, p < .001, partial eta squared = .58. A negotiation scenario gave F(1, 140) = 133.36 and .49, and pictures of basketball players and tornadoes gave F(1, 134) = 50.20 and .27. The same analyses carry a three-way interaction with culture, .11, .13 and .05, with Canadians matching more strongly than Chinese in every case. LeBoeuf and Norton ran the consumer version. A computer crash was attributed to a worldwide virus rather than a cooling fan by 73% of participants when the student lost his job and 56% when he graduated on time, chi-square(1, N = 129) = 4.14, p = .04. A zoo disease was blamed on a bear rather than a rabbit by 36% against 20%, chi-square(1, N = 130) = 4.28, p = .04. Their two conspiracy experiments are the weakest of the set. An assassination in a small country was attributed to a conspiracy by 76% when war followed and 54% when peace did, chi-square(1, N = 74) = 3.80, p = .05, and a version using the Kennedy assassination gave 75% against 64%, chi-square(1, N = 224) = 3.69, p = .055. In a further experiment, matching disappeared among participants first asked to write about a time the world seemed predictable, 43% against 41%, while those who wrote about unpredictability still showed it, 44% against 20%, chi-square(1, N = 62) = 4.00, p = .05.

replication.headline: The magnitude-matching inference reproduces across scenarios and two countries with large effects, while the conspiracy version of it holds in one of the four studies that varied consequence size and only among people asked to take the victims' side.
replication.detail: Van Prooijen and van Dijk ran five studies on consequence size and conspiracy belief. Study 1 gave 71 Dutch students a bogus report of an opposition leader in Benin who either died in a car crash or survived it. Conspiracy belief was higher after the death, 4.18 against 3.45 on a seven-point scale, F(1, 67) = 7.50, p < .01, omega squared = .08, and the authors read this as replicating LeBoeuf and Norton, Leman and Cinnirella, and McCauley and Jacques. The main effect was qualified by an interaction with perspective taking, F(1, 67) = 4.47, omega squared = .05: consequence size moved belief among participants told to take the perspective of Benin's citizens, F(1, 67) = 11.75, and not among those told to be objective, F < 1. In Study 2, with 79 participants and a shooting instead of a crash, the consequence-size term was flat, beta = .10, t(76) = 0.89, and only the interaction with perspective-taking ability reached the threshold, beta = .26, t(75) = 2.40. Study 3 measured perceived consequences of the 11 September attacks among 80 participants and again found no main effect, beta = .08, t(77) = 0.69. Study 4, with 114 participants and a third perspective condition, reported the interaction, F(2, 108) = 4.02, and no consequence-size main effect; in the condition taking the perspective of an average Dutch citizen the means ran backwards, 4.18 after the death against 4.66 after the survival, F(1, 108) = 2.06, p = .15. Study 5 held consequences constant and does not test the claim. Nothing resembling a preregistered or multi-laboratory replication of the conspiracy result was located.

study.cite: van Prooijen, J.-W., & van Dijk, E. (2014). When consequence size predicts belief in conspiracy theories: The moderating role of perspective taking. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 55, 63-73.

limits: No effect sizes are printed in the structured fields. The two literatures report partial eta squared, omega squared and chi-squares on binary choices, and pairing any of them would invent a comparison no paper makes. The experimental base is also small. Every cell in the studies read here holds tens of people, and the conspiracy experiments turn on chi-squares of 3.69 and 3.80 in samples of 224 and 74. Several documents could not be obtained. McCauley and Jacques is described here only through van Prooijen and van Dijk, who report that its participants read about a man shooting at a president who either died or lived and were asked whether he acted alone or belonged to an organised group, and that suspicion of a conspiracy was higher when the president died. Leman and Cinnirella's 2007 paper sits behind the British Psychological Society's paywall with no repository copy recorded by Unpaywall, and its abstract was read from the Semantic Scholar record rather than the publisher. LeBoeuf and Norton's per-experiment statistics come from the authors' March 2010 draft posted at Wharton, not from the 2012 journal version, whose published abstract was read separately and matches the draft's account. Spina's figures come from the 2009 dissertation rather than the 2010 article, whose abstract alone was read at Europe PMC. Ebel-Lam, Fabrigar, MacDonald and Jones, whose plane-crash scenario is the study usually cited for magnitude matching in social explanation, was blocked by the publisher and is described through Spina's summary of it. The search covered Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar, and turned up no replication attempt indexed under proportionality bias, no registered report, and no meta-analysis of consequence size.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat the bias as an explanation of conspiracy belief in general. What the experiments manipulate is one inference about one vignette, made by students who mostly held no prior view of the event, and Leman and Cinnirella report that this inference was unrelated to how much a participant believed in real conspiracy theories. A second error is to quote the effect as settled. Of the four van Prooijen and van Dijk studies that varied or measured consequence size, one produced the plain effect, two produced nothing without a moderator, and one produced a reversal in the group asked to take an uninvolved country's perspective. The bias is also described as a human universal. Canadians in Spina's studies matched cause to effect more strongly than Chinese participants did in all three scenarios, and both groups matched, so the finding is a difference in degree rather than a bias one culture lacks. LeBoeuf and Norton's own result cuts against permanence too, since a short writing task about a predictable world removed the matching entirely. The Kennedy experiment is often retold as showing that people believe in a conspiracy when told the assassination prolonged the Vietnam War. The gap it reports is 75% against 64%, at p = .055. Finally, proportionality bias and apophenia are run together in popular accounts. Pattern perception concerns finding structure in noise; this concerns sizing a cause to an outcome whose size is already known, and evidence for one does not carry to the other.

sources.text: Leman, P. J., & Cinnirella, M. (2007). A major event has a major cause: Evidence for the role of heuristics in reasoning about conspiracy theories. Social Psychological Review, 9(2), 18-28. Publisher access blocked and no open copy recorded by Unpaywall; the abstract was read from the Semantic Scholar record for this DOI.

McCauley, C., & Jacques, S. (1979). The popularity of conspiracy theories of presidential assassination: A Bayesian analysis. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(5), 637-644. Bibliographic record verified at Crossref; the paper itself was not obtained and is described on this page through van Prooijen and van Dijk (2014).

LeBoeuf, R. A., & Norton, M. I. (2012). Consequence-Cause Matching: Looking to the Consequences of Events to Infer Their Causes. Journal of Consumer Research, 39(1), 128-141. Published abstract read at Oxford Academic; all per-experiment statistics quoted here were read from the authors' March 2010 draft at https://marketing.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/Cause_Effect_Similarity.pdf.

Spina, R. R. (2009). Cultural Differences in Expectations of a Correspondence in Magnitude between Events and their Causes. Doctoral thesis, Queen's University, Kingston. Full text read; the source for every Spina figure on this page.

Spina, R. R., Ji, L.-J., Guo, T., Zhang, Z., Li, Y., & Fabrigar, L. (2010). Cultural differences in the representativeness heuristic: expecting a correspondence in magnitude between cause and effect. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 36(5), 583-597. The published version of the dissertation above; read as the abstract at Europe PMC, which states that Canadians expected correspondence in magnitude more than Chinese did.

van Prooijen, J.-W., & van Dijk, E. (2014). When consequence size predicts belief in conspiracy theories: The moderating role of perspective taking. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 55, 63-73. Full text read from the author's copy at janwillemvanprooijen.com.

Basic and Applied Social Psychology, 32(4), 348-359. Blocked by the publisher and not read; named because its plane-crash scenario is the study usually cited for magnitude matching in social explanation.

Leman, P. J., & Cinnirella, M. (2013). Beliefs in conspiracy theories and the need for cognitive closure. Frontiers in Psychology, 4, 378. Full text read at PubMed Central. The authors' later work, and it does not manipulate consequence size; it cites the 2007 heuristic without retesting it.
